article.title: Why Writing Sounds Generic: The Psychology Behind It
article.author: Team Lexi
article.plain_text: Nobody wakes up and says, “Today, I’m going to write something generic.” And yet — somehow — we often do. That’s often why writing sounds generic—even when the intention is to sound clear, professional, or helpful. This shows up everywhere. From emails and landing pages to AI-generated replies that all start to sound eerily similar. Why generic language feels safe It’s not laziness. It’s psychology. Our brains are wired to default to familiar language when we want to avoid friction, mistakes, or standing out. Generic phrases are mental shortcuts. They save energy, reduce risk, signal safety. Saying “We apologize for the inconvenience” feels safe because everyone says it. And if everyone says it, it must be fine. However, what feels safe to the writer often feels invisible to the reader. This is one of the main reasons why writing sounds generic, especially in professional, marketing, and AI-assisted communication. Why writing sounds generic in the first place? Three reasons 1. The curse of knowledge: once we know something, we assume others know it too. We lose the ability to imagine the gaps in their understanding. That’s how we end up skipping context our reader actually needs. 2. It’s also about safety bias—our brain prefers familiarity, even if it renders us invisible. The easy path feels less risky than being different. Neutral language feels safer than taking a clear position. 3, Add cognitive economy, our brain’s instinct to reuse what’s already stored, and suddenly clichés and templates aren’t just sloppy writing, they’re survival strategies. Templates feel efficient in the moment, but over time they erase voice. As a result, the very instincts that kept our ancestors safe in groups now make our writing lifeless today. This explains why writing sounds generic even when people genuinely try to be clear, helpful, or professional. Breaking out of generic isn’t just a stylistic move, it’s challenging how your brain wants to protect you. That’s why advice alone rarely works because the resistance isn’t technical, it’s cognitive. And that’s exactly why we built Lexi: to disrupt your autopilot and return language to where its power truly lies: at the intersection of clarity and authenticity. Lexi is designed to interrupt default phrases, surface blind spots, and force specificity back into writing. Once you understand why writing sounds generic, it becomes much easier to catch yourself before default language takes over. Side-box: Why our brain pushes us into generic This bias is one of the psychological reasons why writing sounds generic, especially when speed and efficiency matter. Curse of knowledge: Once you know something, it’s almost impossible to imagine not knowing it — so you assume others “get it” too. Result: you skip details your reader actually needs. 🔗Harvard Business Review

synthesis: Final verdict: This is a thoughtful, readable piece that convincingly explains why writing sounds generic by pointing to mental shortcuts and cognitive biases, but it stops short of fully helping readers escape the “autopilot” that produces generic phrasing. Biggest strengths: an engaging, relatable opening and a clear application of psychological concepts that give readers a real reason to care; a warm, conversational tone that balances authority and approachability. Biggest weaknesses: the structure is weak—sparse headings, abrupt transitions and some dense paragraphs hurt scannability—and the article lacks vivid, concrete examples or before/after rewrites, so much advice remains abstract and occasionally buzzwordy. Top 3 actionable recommendations (prioritised): 1) Add clear section headings and signposts and break dense paragraphs to improve flow and skimmability; 2) Insert vivid, short examples or a brief anecdote plus before/after rewrites of generic lines to make concepts concrete; 3) Strip jargon by replacing buzzwords with plain phrasing and end with a concise, practical checklist (3–5 edits readers can apply immediately) to help disrupt the writing “autopilot.”
